  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
Kwame was sixty-eight years old, a widower who had spent his life as a dancer—first with a small modern company in Chicago, later teaching at a community studio. He had always moved through the world with the quiet confidence of someone who trusted his body completely. That trust shattered on a rainy Tuesday evening two years ago, driving home from a rehearsal. He was stopped at a red light when a delivery truck ran the intersection and slammed into the driver’s side of his sedan. The impact spun the car across two lanes. Kwame remembers the headlights of oncoming traffic, the screech of metal, the smell of gasoline. He remembers nothing after that until he was in the ambulance, a paramedic pressing gauze to his forehead. The police report later described the extrication, the collapsed door, the ten minutes he was trapped. Kwame cannot tell that story to himself as a clear sequence. When he tries deliberately to recall what happened between the impact and the ambulance, he finds only fragments—a sharp pain in his ribs, someone shouting, a sense of crushing pressure—and the rest is simply missing. He knows he was there, but the memory feels like a handful of photographs from an album that has lost all its pages.

In the weeks after the accident, Kwame began to notice changes he could not quite name. He stopped accepting invitations from the friends he had socialised with before the crash. They meant well, but being around them felt wrong—they talked about normal things, and he could not find a way to be present in those conversations. He started turning down invitations to dance events, then to any gathering outside his apartment. The thought of walking out the front door and crossing the street felt dangerous, though he could not say exactly what he feared. When he did go out, he found himself scanning every room for a place where his back would be against a wall. If there was no such spot, his shoulders would knot up and his breathing would turn shallow. He became sensitive to unexpected sounds: a car horn, a door slamming, a dropped tray in a café—each one sent a jolt through him, and for a few seconds he would be back in the car, waiting for the impact.

He had always been a patient man, but now delays took on a different meaning. If a rehearsal started late, if a bus did not arrive on time, if a phone call was not returned promptly, he assumed something bad was happening. His mind would race with scenarios: an accident, an injury, a death. Intellectually he knew this was unlikely, but his body did not listen. And his body—the instrument he had relied on for fifty years—had become unreliable. He could no longer trust it to do what he asked. A simple plié felt shaky; his left knee would stiffen unpredictably. Kwame began to doubt himself in ways that were new and corrosive. He questioned every small decision—which route to take, what time to leave, where to sit in a room. What if he chose wrong again? What if his judgment was permanently broken?

He had gone to therapy at his doctor’s urging. In the first few sessions he tried to talk about the accident, but each time he felt his throat close, his hands go cold. He found himself deliberately turning his mind away from anything the therapist had mentioned between sessions, as if the very words carried a contagion. He stopped attending after four appointments, telling himself he was too busy. The truth was that he could not bear to open that door.

It was his daughter who finally persuaded him to try again. She had noticed he was no longer teaching, no longer visiting his late wife’s grave, no longer even taking walks. She sat with him one Sunday afternoon and told him, gently, that she was worried. Kwame agreed to come back to therapy because he could see the sadness in her eyes—and because, alone in his apartment with his back against the wall of his living room, he had begun to wonder if this was all that was left. He did not expect to recover his memory or his trust. He hoped, very quietly, that he might at least feel less afraid of the sound of a door closing.
